name: plot.boot
title: Plots of the output of a bootstrap simulation

origin.description: Draw a histogram of bootstrap replicates and a Q-Q plot against normal or chi-squared quantiles. Optionally add a jackknife-after-bootstrap plot.
origin.usage:
plot.boot(x, index = 1, t0 = NULL, t = NULL, jack = FALSE,
     qdist = "norm", nclass = NULL, df, ...)

arguments.name: index
arguments.text: Which column of the bootstrap statistics to plot. Ignored when t is supplied.

arguments.name: t0
arguments.text: The original statistic. Defaults to boot.out$t0[index] unless t is supplied, in which case it defaults to NULL and no vertical line is drawn.

arguments.name: t
arguments.text: Replicates to plot. The default is boot.out$t[, index].

arguments.name: jack
arguments.text: If TRUE, add a jackknife-after-bootstrap plot under the histogram and the Q-Q plot.

arguments.name: qdist
arguments.text: Reference distribution for the Q-Q plot: "norm" or "chisq". Anything else warns and uses the normal.

arguments.name: nclass
arguments.text: Number of histogram classes. The default is the integer between 10 and 100 closest to ceiling(length(t) / 25).
Passed to jack.after.boot when jack is TRUE.

origin.details: When t0 is known, one histogram breakpoint is placed at t0 and the classes have equal width. The Q-Q plot uses quantiles qnorm((1:R)/(R+1)), or chi-squared quantiles, against the order statistics of the finite replicates. The normal reference line has intercept mean(t) and slope sqrt(var(t)). The chi-squared line is the unit line.
origin.example:
# We fit an exponential model to the air-conditioning data and use
# that for a parametric bootstrap.  Then we look at plots of the
# resampled means.
air.rg <- function(data, mle) rexp(length(data), 1/mle)

air.boot <- boot(aircondit$hours, mean, R = 999, sim = "parametric",
                 ran.gen = air.rg, mle = mean(aircondit$hours))
plot(air.boot)

translation.description: Draw a histogram of bootstrap replicates and a Q-Q plot with Matplotlib. The returned dict is the series the figure is built from.
translation.usage: plot_boot(x, index=1, t0=None, t=None, jack=False, qdist="norm", nclass=None, df=None, **kwargs)

arguments.name: index
arguments.text: 1-based column of t to plot. Ignored when t is supplied.

arguments.name: t0
arguments.text: Original statistic. When t is omitted this defaults to t0[index]. When t is supplied and t0 is omitted, no vertical line is drawn.

arguments.name: t
arguments.text: Replicates to plot instead of column index of x.t.

arguments.name: jack
arguments.text: If true, add a jackknife-after-bootstrap panel under the histogram and the Q-Q plot.

arguments.name: qdist
arguments.text: "norm" or "chisq". Any other string warns and uses the normal.

arguments.name: nclass
arguments.text: Number of histogram classes. The default follows ceiling(length(t) / 25), bounded by 10 and 100.

arguments.name: df
arguments.text: Degrees of freedom when qdist is "chisq".

arguments.name: kwargs
arguments.text: Passed to jack_after_boot when jack is true.

translation.details: Breakpoints put t0 on a boundary and use equal widths, matching the R formula. Counts use right-closed bins and include the left edge in the first bin. Theoretical quantiles are qnorm((1:R)/(R+1)) or the chi-squared quantile at those probabilities. The normal line is mean(t) + sqrt(var(t)) * quantile. Matplotlib draws the bars, the points, and the line.
translation.value: A dict with breaks, counts, density, qq_x, qq_y, line_intercept, and line_slope. figure is the Matplotlib figure.
translation.example:
from boot.resample import boot, plot_boot
from boot.rng import set_seed
import numpy as np

def stat(d, i):
    i = np.asarray(i, dtype=int)
    return float(np.mean(np.asarray(d)[i - 1]))

set_seed(1)
result = boot(np.arange(1, 11), stat, R=50)
series = plot_boot(result)
print(series["counts"])
